overview: Aruba's street food scene centers around late-night food trucks, known locally as truck di pan, and casual snack counters. Visitors can find Dutch and Indonesian influences alongside Caribbean staples, with vendors serving up hearty portions of ribs, fries, and peanut sauce. Morning markets and bakeries are the place to grab freshly fried pastechi before heading to the beach.

overview: The region is known for its seafood, often sold directly from boats or at harborside markets. overview: Street food in the Galápagos is centered in Puerto Ayora on Santa Cruz Island, where a single street transforms into an open-air dining area each evening. Local stalls serve fresh seafood, including whole grilled fish, lobster, and ceviche, alongside rice and plantains. The experience is casual and focused on the day's catch.

The summer produce fades, and outdoor market stalls thin out as the weather cools. Autumn brings a few harvest-focused stalls selling early cured meats and late-season apples before the winter snows arrive.

December brings holiday markets to towns like Chur and Sion, featuring stalls pouring hot Glühwein and scraping melted raclette onto bread. Street vendors sell heissi Marroni (roasted chestnuts) to skiers and shoppers.

overview: Tierra del Fuego has a modest street food scene centered around casual food trucks and local fairs in Ushuaia and Rio Grande. Visitors can find stalls serving choripán, baked empanadas, and occasionally local seafood like centolla (king crab) during summer events. The outdoor eating culture is most active in the warmer months when food trucks operate reliably near the ports.

overview: The town of Uyuni serves as the gateway to the salt flats, and visitors can explore Mercado Central for casual meals of llama meat or quinoa. Stalls around the town center sell baked salteñas in the morning and hot api with buñuelos to combat the freezing Andean nights.
months: Mercado Central is the hub for daytime eating, featuring hearty soups and roasted meats. In the evenings, vendors set up near the main plaza to sell grilled anticuchos and sweet api. The high altitude brings freezing nights, making hot street snacks a staple.

overview: Yellowstone National Park has no street food or food halls, but its gateway towns host modest summer farmers' markets. Visitors can find regional specialties like huckleberry preserves, elk jerky, and fresh produce at weekly outdoor stalls in West Yellowstone and Jackson. The short summer season is the only time these markets operate.

overview: Victoria Falls and the surrounding towns feature modest local markets where visitors can try Zimbabwean staples. Open-air stalls and community hubs like Chinotimba Market host vendors selling roasted corn, dried kapenta, and seasonal macimbi. The dry winter months provide the most reliable conditions for browsing outdoor food stands.

The main draw is the Zion Canyon Farmers Market in Springdale, where vendors sell local produce, baked goods, and ready-to-eat snacks. Options around Bryce Canyon are restricted to standard cafes and grocery stores.
